title: Grandma's Garden Pond
sum: Zoe and her little brother Max spend a week at Grandma Bea's, keeping a nature journal of who visits the garden pond, and at last get close to Captain Plop the frog.

cast.d: a nine-year-old girl who keeps the nature journal and likes neat tables
cast.look: a nine-year-old girl with a long brown braid, a striped T-shirt, denim shorts and a green notebook

cast.d: Zoe's six-year-old brother, loud and funny, who can't sit still
cast.look: a six-year-old boy with curly blond hair, a dinosaur T-shirt and muddy sneakers

cast.d: their grandmother, who has a small round pond in her garden and loves a joke
cast.look: an older woman with short white hair, a wide straw hat, a blue apron and glasses on a cord

cast.d: a green frog who lives in the pond
cast.look: a green frog about the size of a grown-up's palm, with gold eyes and a pale yellow throat

cast.d: the orange cat from next door
cast.look: a round orange tabby cat with white paws

p: Grandma Bea's pond sat at the bottom of her garden, round and about 2 meters across. Seven lily pads floated on top, and tall reeds grew along the back. At the front, a flat gray stone sat right at the water's edge, warm from the sun.

Zoe and Max had come to stay for a whole week in July. Max ran down the path first, and his sneakers went slap, slap, slap. Something hit the water with a loud PLOP, and rings spread across the pond until they touched the edge.
Grandma came down the path behind them with a bowl of peas. “That's the pond's doorbell,” she said before anyone could ask. “Every time somebody comes running down to the water, it goes plop.”

Max lay down on his belly and stared into the water. All he could see were a few bubbles and the green bottoms of the lily pads. “I want to see who lives in there,” he said, with his chin in the grass.

“So do I,” said Grandma, and sat down on the bench with the bowl on her lap. “I'd love to know who comes to my pond, but I only get to watch it at breakfast.” She pulled a green notebook from her apron pocket and handed it to Zoe. “A nature journal. Write down whoever comes to the water.”
Zoe sat down in the grass at the edge of the pond. “Come and sit on the bank with me, Max,” she said, and Max looked all around. “What bank? I don't see any money.”

Grandma laughed so hard that two peas rolled off her lap. “Not that kind of bank,” she said, and pointed at the grass along the water's edge. Max patted the grass under his chin. “A bank with no money is a bad bank.”
“Whoever made that plop is hiding now,” said Grandma. “Keep very still, and he'll come back up to look at you.” Zoe's watch said 4:05, and she held the notebook on her knees without moving a finger.

Max kept still too, for about one minute. Then he pulled up grass, hummed and counted the seven lily pads out loud. When a bee buzzed past his ear, he jumped up and flapped both arms like a windmill. Zoe shushed him, so he flopped onto his back and watched the clouds instead.
The water smelled green and a little muddy. A blue dragonfly hovered over the reeds like a tiny helicopter. Zoe's left foot fell asleep, but she kept it right where it was.

At last, next to the biggest lily pad, two bumps rose out of the water. They were gold and shiny like marbles, with a dark green shadow underneath. The rest of the frog stayed hidden. Without moving her head, Zoe peeked at her watch, which now said 4:17.

“See how his eyes sit right on top of his head?” Grandma whispered. “He can hide his body under the water and still look out, like you peeking over your blanket at night.” The gold eyes blinked, and Zoe hardly dared to breathe.

Then Max sat up fast and shouted, “Where is he?” With a loud PLOP, the eyes were gone, and rings rolled across the pond. Max's mouth fell open. “He rang the doorbell again!” “No,” said Zoe, “you did.”

Zoe opened the green notebook and wrote Monday at the top of the first page. Under it she wrote Visitors: 1 frog (mostly eyes), and drew two gold marbles on the water. “Write his name too,” said Max, leaning over her shoulder. “His name is Captain Plop.”

art.s: A girl with a long brown braid and her curly-haired little brother sit on the grassy bank of a small round garden pond with seven lily pads, while two gold frog eyes peek above the water and their grandmother in a straw hat shells peas on a bench.

q.q: Draw Captain Plop hiding in the pond, the way Zoe first saw him. Which part of him stays above the water?
look: only the eyes above the water
the body hidden under the water
a lily pad or ripples nearby
q.e: Eyes on top, body hidden. That's how a frog can hide and watch at the same time!

q.q: Max thought a bank was a place for money. What does bank mean at the pond?
c: the land along the edge of the water
a box that keeps coins safe
the deepest part of the pond
a flat stone in the water
q.e: Bank has two meanings. At a pond, it's the grassy land along the edge, the kind Grandma pointed at.

q.q: Zoe started waiting at 4:05. How many minutes did she wait before the gold eyes came up?
q.e: From 4:05 to 4:17 is 12 minutes. That's a long time to sit still!

p: On Tuesday, Zoe made a plan: three watches a day, at 8:30, at noon and at 6:00. Each watch would last 10 minutes. Grandma lent her the kitchen timer, a plastic chicken that ticked when you turned its head.

Zoe ruled a table in the green notebook and wrote Bees, Birds, Dragonflies, Frogs and Other down the side. Every visitor would get one tally mark. The fifth mark in each group would go across the other four. “It looks like a gate,” said Max, “with four cows inside.”

At 8:30 they sat down on the bank, and Zoe turned the chicken's head. Tick, tick, tick. Three bees landed on the wet stones at the shallow end to drink, and Zoe made three marks. Then a robin hopped down to the water and splashed.

Max grabbed the pencil and gave the robin a mark. The bird shook itself and hopped onto the grass to tug at a worm. Then it came back to splash again, so Max made another mark. When the robin came back a third time, he made a third.

“Max, that's one robin,” Zoe whispered. “You can't count the same bird three times.” Max folded his arms and whispered back, “But it came three times, and I watched it.” Their whispers got louder and louder until the robin flew off to the fence.

Grandma came out with her coffee. “So what are you two trying to find out?” “Who visits the pond,” said Zoe, “and how often they come.” Grandma pointed her cup at the fence, where the robin was already eyeing the water again.

Zoe looked at the robin, and then at Max's three marks. “So it's three visits, and Max is right,” she said, and her ears went hot. At the top of the page she wrote a new rule: Every trip to the water is a visit. Max drew a big star next to his marks.

By noon the sun was high, and the path was hot under their bare feet. Zoe turned the chicken's head and made a prediction. “There will be more bees now, because it's hot and bees get thirsty too.” Max had one too: “A whale.”

No whale came, but Zoe was right about the bees. They crowded side by side on the wet stones at the shallow end. Each one drank and zipped away over the fence, and another took its place. Zoe's pencil went scritch, scritch, scritch, and when the chicken dinged, she had 12 bee marks.
“Where do they all go?” Max asked. “Home to their hive,” said Grandma. “On a hot day, bees spread water inside the hive and fan it with their wings. As the water dries, the hive cools down.”
Max licked his arm and blew on it. “Hey, it's cold!” “Same trick,” said Grandma, “but the bees are better at it.” Max tried it on his other arm, just in case.

At 6:00 the garden was shady and cool, and only 2 bees came to the stones. A dragonfly zipped over the lily pads and back again. Captain Plop floated by the reeds with only his gold eyes showing. He had been right there at 8:30 and at noon, and he never came or went.

Zoe tapped her pencil on the Frogs row and frowned. Every trip to the water was a visit, but Captain Plop never made a trip. So was he one visit, or none, or a hundred? She drew a small question mark for each watch and closed the notebook. The chicken timer sat on top of it like a hen on an egg.

art.s: At noon, a girl and a little boy sit on a pond bank with a chicken-shaped kitchen timer and a notebook full of tally marks, while a row of honeybees drinks from wet stones at the shallow end and a robin watches from the fence.

q.q: At noon, Zoe made 12 marks in the Bees row. Draw them the way she did. Remember the gates of five!
q.e: Five, ten, eleven, twelve. Gates of five make big counts easy to read!

q.q: Why did so many bees come to the pond at noon?
q.a: It was the hottest time of day. The bees were thirsty, and they carried water home to cool their hive.
q.e: On hot days, bees drink and carry water home. They spread it in the hive and fan it, and it cools the hive, like your wet arm when you blow on it.

q.q: Zoe's new rule said, “Every trip to the water is a visit.” What does visit mean in her rule?
c: one time an animal comes to the water
one animal, no matter how often it comes
a week of staying at Grandma's house
ten minutes of watching the pond
q.e: Visit can mean a long stay, like Zoe's week at Grandma's. In her rule, it means one trip to the water, so the robin made three visits.

p: On Wednesday, Max had a new plan. He filled his red sand bucket with pond water and set it on the bank. “I'm going to catch Captain Plop and keep him in my room,” he said, “and feed him cookies every day.”

Grandma looked at the bucket over the top of her glasses. “Captain Plop has a job,” she said, “so he can't be a pet.” Max made a face that meant frogs didn't have jobs. “Watch him tonight,” said Grandma, “and you'll see.”

At 6:00 the three of them sat on the bank in the warm, still air. Mosquitoes whined around Grandma's ankles, and she slapped at them with her hat. “Five bites already,” she said, “and they're not done yet.”

Captain Plop was sitting on the flat gray stone, and his throat puffed in and out like a tiny balloon. Zoe wrote Snacks at the top of a clean page and turned the chicken's head to 10. A fat black fly landed on the stone, a hand's width from his nose.

There was a wet little snap, and the fly was gone before Zoe even saw the frog's mouth open. She made one mark under Snacks. “Did you SEE that?” Max shouted, and with a PLOP, Captain Plop was gone too.

“Frogs don't like shouting,” said Grandma, and Max clapped both hands over his mouth. When the gold eyes came up again, Grandma leaned close. “Watch his tongue this time. It's stuck on at the front of his mouth, and it flips out like a party blower.”

Near the end of the 10 minutes, a little green grasshopper landed on a lily pad. Captain Plop swam closer, barely making a ripple, and snapped it up too. This time Zoe saw the tongue, a flash of pink, out and back. She made a second mark, and the chicken dinged.

“Two in ten minutes,” said Grandma. “What about a whole hour?” Zoe counted on her fingers: an hour was 60 minutes, so that was six tens. Before she could finish, Max whispered as loud as he could, “A hundred!”
“Not quite,” said Grandma, rubbing a new bite on her ankle. “But it's a lot of bugs, and frogs eat mosquitoes too.”
Max looked at Captain Plop and then at his bucket. “So he eats the bugs that bite you.” “That's his job,” said Grandma. “He pays his rent in bugs.”

On a new page, Zoe drew a clump of grass, the grasshopper and Captain Plop in a row. The grasshopper ate grass, and Captain Plop ate the grasshopper. So she drew an arrow from each one to the one that ate it.

“Who eats Captain Plop?” Max asked in a very small voice. “A heron might try,” said Grandma, “a tall gray bird with long legs and a beak like chopsticks. That's why he plops whenever something big comes near.”

Zoe drew one more arrow, and a tall gray bird at the end of the row. Max stared at the heron and said, “Poor Captain Plop.” “Don't worry about him,” said Grandma. “He's the best plopper on this street.”

Max carried his bucket to the shallow end. For a second, Zoe thought he would try to catch Captain Plop after all. Instead, he poured the water back into the pond a little at a time. Out slid two tadpoles he hadn't known he'd caught, each with two tiny back legs. “Keep up the good work, Captain,” Max whispered.

art.s: In warm evening light, a green frog on a flat gray stone at the edge of a garden pond snaps up a fly with its long tongue, while a little boy holding a red sand bucket shouts in surprise and his sister draws a food chain in a green notebook.

q.q: Captain Plop caught 2 bugs in 10 minutes. If he kept going like that, how many bugs would he catch in one hour?
q.e: An hour has six 10-minute parts. Six times 2 is 12.

q.q: Draw the moment Captain Plop snapped up the fly. Give Max a speech bubble with the words he shouted.
look: the frog's tongue reaching the fly
a speech bubble with Max's words
q.e: What a snap! Your speech bubble lets us hear Max shout.

q.q: Which food chain did Zoe draw in her journal?
c: grass → grasshopper → frog → heron
grass → frog → grasshopper → heron
grasshopper → grass → heron → frog
heron → grass → frog → grasshopper
q.e: The grasshopper eats grass, the frog eats the grasshopper, and a heron eats frogs. Each arrow points to the eater.

p: On Thursday, Zoe woke up to a drumming sound on the roof. When she ran to the window, the whole garden was gray, and the pond was jumping with raindrops.
Downstairs, Zoe flopped into a kitchen chair and said, “My count is ruined.” Grandma poured the milk. “Rain doesn't ruin a count. Rain is part of the count.”

After breakfast, Grandma took them out under her big umbrella to check the rain gauge. It was a clear plastic tube on a post, marked in millimeters, and she had emptied it the night before. Now the water came up to the line marked 6. “Six already,” said Grandma, “and it's still coming down.”
Back inside, Grandma dried her glasses on her apron. “So what will we see today, and why?” “No bees,” said Zoe, “because a big raindrop can knock a bee right out of the air.”
“More frogs,” said Max, before it was even his turn, “because frogs love being wet.” Zoe wrote both predictions on a clean page, under Thursday.

At 8:30 Grandma set her binoculars on the kitchen windowsill. Zoe pressed her nose to the glass, and Max held the chicken timer. Rain made little rings all over the pond, but nobody drank at the wet stones and nobody splashed. When the timer dinged, the Bees row was still empty.
“Zero,” said Zoe, and frowned at the blank row. “Zero is a number too,” said Grandma, “so write it down.” Zoe wrote a big 0 and drew a raindrop next to it.

At noon, something orange moved under the bench. It was Pickles, the cat from next door, hiding from the rain. He crept to the pond and patted the water with one white paw, then shook it hard and stomped home. Zoe put one mark in the Other row.

By 6:00 the rain had slowed to a drizzle, and Zoe opened the window a crack so they could listen. Gunk! A deep sound came from the reeds, like someone plucking a loose guitar string. Then another gunk came from the flat stone, and another from the lily pads.

When Zoe lifted the binoculars, there was Captain Plop on the flat stone, with his pale yellow throat puffing. Another frog sat on a lily pad, and a third sat halfway up the bank, far from the water. “Captain Plop has friends!” Max whispered.

Grandma pointed at the frog on the bank. “On a sunny day, he'd dry out up there. A frog's skin has to stay wet, and he even drinks through it.” “I was right again,” said Max, and poked Zoe with his elbow.

After supper, they ran out under the umbrella one more time. The water in the rain gauge was up to 21 now. “No watering for me tomorrow,” said Grandma, tapping the tube. “Even the pond got a free drink.”
At the kitchen table, Zoe turned to the page she had started that morning, with Thursday at the top. Grandma leaned over her shoulder. “That's the day, but what's the page about?”

Zoe looked at the big 0 in the Bees row and thought about the three frogs in the drizzle. Under Thursday, she wrote a title: No Bees, Three Frogs. Max read it out loud. Then he took the pencil and added one word underneath in big letters: GUNK.

art.s: On a rainy day, a girl with binoculars and her little brother watch a garden pond through a kitchen window, while three green frogs sit on a stone, a lily pad and the grassy bank, and an orange cat shakes a wet paw by a rain gauge.

q.q: Draw Zoe's rainy-day journal page. Give it a title that tells what the whole page is about.
look: a title that tells the big idea
the frogs, or the big 0 for bees
q.e: A good title tells the big idea in a few words. Yours does the job!

q.q: Why could the frogs sit out of the water on the rainy day?
q.a: Frogs need wet skin. The rain kept everything wet, so they didn't dry out.
q.e: A frog's skin has to stay damp. Frogs even drink through it, so rain is perfect frog weather.

q.q: Grandma checked the rain gauge twice. How much rain fell between the two checks?
c: 6 mm
15 mm
21 mm
27 mm
q.e: It went from 6 up to 21. And 21 take away 6 is 15, so 15 mm of rain fell.

p: On Saturday morning, the green notebook was fat with tally marks. Zoe spread it out on the kitchen table and counted four days of watching, row by row. The bees had the most visits by far, with 40.
Grandma found a sheet of big-square graph paper for a bar graph. Zoe counted the squares across, and there were only 12. “Forty won't fit,” she said, “not if one square means one visit.”
Zoe chewed her pencil for a while, and then she sat up straight. “What if one square means 5 visits?” At the bottom of the page, she drew a key: one square = 5 visits.

The bee bar came out yellow and 8 squares long. Max counted it by fives, all the way to 40. The bird bar was red and stopped at 4, and the dragonfly bar was blue and only 3 squares long. Other got one gray square: Pickles, a squirrel and three wasps made 5.

Then Zoe got to the Frogs row, which was full of question marks, one for every watch. “Captain Plop never comes or goes,” she said, “so how am I supposed to count him?” Grandma only shrugged, so Zoe left the frog bar empty and went out for one last watch.

At noon Max went down the path first, and he stopped so fast that Zoe bumped into him. On the flat gray stone sat six tiny frogs, each one about as long as Zoe's thumb. Max opened his mouth to shout, then clapped a hand over it.

Max remembered the doorbell. He got down on his hands and knees and crept toward the stone as slow as a snail. Zoe crawled after him, but the little frogs didn't move. Behind them, two gold eyes came up out of the water.

“Froglets,” Grandma whispered from the bench. “This spring they were tadpoles. They grew back legs first, and then front legs.” Zoe leaned closer and saw that each tiny frog still had a stub of a tail.
“Where's the rest of the tail?” Max whispered. “Their bodies use it up, like a packed lunch,” said Grandma, “and now they breathe air, so out they come.”
Max looked from the froglets to Captain Plop, and his eyes went wide. “They hatched here and grew up here, so they don't visit the pond at all. They live here!”
Zoe sat back on her heels. No wonder the Frogs row was all question marks. She and Max backed away on their knees, and not one froglet jumped.

Back in the kitchen, Zoe wrote across the empty Frogs row in big letters: NOT VISITORS, THEY LIVE HERE. Under it she added 3 big frogs and 6 froglets. Grandma taped the graph to the fridge and stood back to look at it. “So bees are visitors, like you two,” she said, “and frogs live here, like me. Only greener.”

That evening Max lay on his belly next to the flat gray stone. Captain Plop sat on top of it, nose to nose with him, and neither of them moved. Zoe drew them both in the green notebook, and nobody rang the doorbell once.

art.s: A little boy on his hands and knees creeps toward a flat gray stone at the edge of a garden pond where six tiny froglets sit, while a frog's gold eyes peek out of the water behind them, his sister follows close behind, and their grandmother watches from a bench.

q.q: Max said the frogs don't visit the pond. What did he mean?
q.a: The frogs hatched and grew up in the pond. It's their home, so they don't come and go.
q.e: Bees fly in for a drink and fly home. The frogs were born in the pond, so they aren't visitors.

q.q: Zoe's dragonfly bar was 3 squares long. How many visits is that?
q.e: Each square means 5 visits. Three squares: 5, 10, 15.

q.q: Draw how a tadpole turns into a frog, one step at a time, the way Grandma told it.
look: a tadpole with a long tail
back legs first, then front legs
a froglet with a short tail stub
q.e: Long tail, back legs, front legs, then a tiny froglet with a stub. That's how the pond babies grew up.

fin.q: Why was it smart for Captain Plop to dive whenever something big came near?
fin.a: Something big might be a heron, and herons eat frogs. Under the water, he could hide.
fin.e: To a frog, something big could be a hungry heron. When Max crept in low and slow, the frogs stayed put.

fin.q: How did Max change from Monday to Saturday?
c: He learned to stay low and still.
He stopped wanting to see the frogs.
He decided frogs make good pets.
He caught Captain Plop in his bucket.
fin.e: On Monday Max jumped up and made Captain Plop dive. By Saturday he crept in slow and quiet, and the frogs stayed.
